Current as of 30 Aug 2026. Authoritative — reasoning for changes lives in the Decision Log.

## Purpose

Produce personalized daily targets for calories, protein, and fiber, with a plain-English explanation. Targets are adjustable forever after.

## Sequencing — targets before logging

**The questions come first, and onboarding cannot be skipped.**

```
Sign in with Apple
  → six questions
  → your targets
  → Today
  → log your first meal, measured against those targets
```

**Ruled 30 Aug 2026, reversing the 20 Aug sequencing.** The reversed version put the first meal before the questions, on the argument that demanding effort before demonstrating value is a bad activation shape. That argument is real and it lost to a simpler one: this app's whole product is a number measured against a target, and a meal logged with no target to measure it against does not show the trick. It shows half of it.

A first entry with no ring, no progress, and nothing scored is a weaker demonstration than the same entry an hour later with a target behind it. The payoff the resequencing wanted to lead with was never available before targets existed.

Six questions is also not ten. The earlier design that provoked the reversal asked ten, and cutting to six is what made the front-loaded flow tolerable.

### What follows from the order

**No skip, no *Not now*, no bridge screen.** A user with no targets can reach onboarding and nothing else. The mobile guard on every signed-in route enforces it, not only the launch gate, because a deep link to Today never runs the launch gate.

`DailyLog.target_version` **is NOT NULL.** No entry can exist before targets do, so a day with nothing to measure against is no longer reachable. The backfill this doc used to require is gone with it. See doc 02.

`onboarding_completed` **is the only onboarding field.** Server-derived, set when the user's first `TargetVersion` is written, never client-writable. There is no second field, because there is no second way to leave.

**The camera prompt moves later**, which is a gain. Under the reversed order a brand-new user met the iOS camera permission prompt within seconds of installing, at the coldest possible moment, with exactly one shot at it. Now they meet it after answering six questions and seeing their own targets. See doc 06.

### The cost, stated plainly

Abandonment during the questions now means the user is back at question one on their next launch, with no way into the app. That is the intended behaviour of a hard gate and it is a real risk: an unexitable flow with a broken step traps everyone who reaches it. Doc 04 describes exactly that trap, from the deleted verify-email stack.

The protection is that all six questions are local and answerable offline. Nothing in the flow waits on a network call except the final target write, and doc 18's deterministic fallback covers the AI step. Any future step that can block must not sit inside this stack.

## The six questions

Everything Mifflin-St Jeor needs, nothing else.

| Field | Type |
| -- | -- |
| Age | int |
| Biological sex | enum |
| Height | int, inches |
| Current weight | decimal, pounds |
| Goal | enum — cut / maintain / gain |
| Activity level | enum — sedentary → very active |

One question per screen. Progress indicator. Back navigation preserves answers.

**US units end to end. Corrected 29 Aug 2026**, reversing a decision made the same day.

Height is entered in feet and inches, weight in pounds, and **those are the units the API takes and the units the server works in**. No conversion in the client.

The first version of this section said the opposite: US units on screen, other units on the wire, with the client converting at its edge. The reasoning was that Mifflin-St Jeor is not defined in pounds and inches, so the formula should get what it wants.

That was backwards. It put a conversion in every client for the convenience of one formula, and it meant the API spoke a unit no screen ever shows. Debugging a request then means converting in your head before you can tell whether a number is sensible.

[MAC-51](https://linear.app/hintology/issue/MAC-51/post-apitargetsproposals-the-deterministic-proposal-no-ai) owns the one conversion the formula needs, inside the function that needs it. Nothing else in the stack converts, and no constant elsewhere is written in anything but pounds.

Height stays **one** control despite feet-and-inches looking like two. Hold total inches as the value, step by one, and format the label as `5'11"`. A second control on that screen would break the one-question-per-screen rule the whole flow is built on.

No units toggle. Nothing in any doc asks for one, and adding it later means a `units` field on `User` plus a preference screen. If someone outside the US complains, that is a real signal rather than a guess.

### Two of the six answers are stored

Added 30 Aug 2026. `sex` and `current_weight_lb` land on `User`; age, height, goal, and activity do not.

The four that are dropped feed Mifflin-St Jeor once and are never wanted again. The two that are kept are needed every time a target is written, including from Settings weeks later, because the server has to bound a protein target against a body weight.

This was found the first time an endpoint tried to save a target and had nothing to check it against. The app had been asking for current weight, using it, and discarding it, while keeping the *goal* weight. Storing the target and forgetting the number it is measured against is backwards.

Whoever computes a proposal writes both fields, so onboarding populates them as a side effect rather than needing a step of its own.

The latest weight only, not a history. A weight log is a real feature and this is not it.

### Moved to settings

Goal weight, timeline, training days per week, and dietary constraints. All improve target quality; none block computing them.

Goal weight is stored as `goal_weight_lb`. It shipped as `goal_weight_kg` in [MAC-28](https://linear.app/hintology/issue/MAC-28/session-endpoints-refresh-sign-out-and-me), before the US units decision, and was renamed with a converting migration on 30 Aug 2026. Nothing computes from it yet: Mifflin-St Jeor does not read it and neither does the clamp. It is a stated intention the model can be given as context, and the rate-of-loss guidance in the rationale is where it earns its place.

**Note:** dietary constraints feed the advice feature, which is weaker without them. Prompt for it when advice is first used, not at signup. That prompt is specified here but not yet drawn — see doc 25.

## Target generation

The decision was to use an AI call. The implementation is a **hybrid**, which keeps the value and drops the failure mode:

1. Compute Mifflin-St Jeor plus activity multiplier deterministically
2. Pass that baseline to the model as context
3. The model adjusts and explains

Arithmetic stays reproducible and free; the model contributes judgment on protein relative to body weight and goal, sensible fiber targets, rate-of-loss guidance, and a readable rationale.

If the model's numbers drift far from the baseline, log it — that's a signal worth watching.

## Server-side guardrails — mandatory

Public app, health-adjacent numbers. AI output is **never** trusted directly:

* Calories clamped to a floor and ceiling by sex and body weight. Reject implausibly low values regardless of what the model says
* Protein clamped to a sane range per pound of body weight
* Fiber clamped to a reasonable daily range
* Out-of-bounds responses fall back to the deterministic formula, and the event is logged
* Response shape validated strictly — request JSON, parse it, reject malformed output rather than pattern-matching prose

**Disclaimer required in the UI:** these are estimates, not medical advice. Non-negotiable for a health-adjacent public app, and App Review looks for it.

### Two ranges, not one

Ruled 29 Aug 2026, resolving a contradiction between this doc and doc 15. Doc 15's `6h` said the server clamps whatever it is given; this doc said adjusting past the safe bounds is permitted. Both were half right.

**The suggested range** is the one above, derived from sex and body weight. AI output is clamped into it, always, with no exception. A user who steps outside it gets an orange warning and their number is saved exactly as typed.

**The absolute range** is wider and nothing crosses it, not the model and not the user. Calories floor at **1,000**. Below that the request is rejected with a `400` rather than clamped, because silently storing a different number than the one someone typed is worse than telling them no. Protein and fiber get the same treatment.

The two ranges answer two different questions. The suggested range asks "is this a sensible target?", and a person is allowed to disagree with the app about their own body. The absolute range asks "is this a target at all?", and nobody gets to disagree, the model included.

One range would have forced a choice between two bad outcomes: clamp everything and someone eating 1,400 under medical supervision cannot record it while the app rewrites their number, or clamp nothing the user typed and someone sets 400.

**Where 1,000 comes from, honestly.** A judgement call, not a clinical citation. Under roughly 800 is medically supervised territory a phone app has no business in, and 1,000 sits below every ordinary aggressive cut while still refusing the genuinely dangerous. The reasoning belongs in a comment above the constant, because this number will get questioned later.

Both ranges are hardcoded constants in the `targets` app, never environment variables. Same reasoning as the JWT lifetimes: a safety-shaped constant should move through a pull request where someone reads the diff, and an env override splits the tested value from the live one.

## Endpoints

```
POST /api/targets/proposals/     answers → proposed targets + rationale (not persisted)
POST /api/targets/               create a new TargetVersion
GET  /api/targets/               every version, newest first
GET  /api/targets/current/       the version in effect now
```

Accepting onboarding targets and manually adjusting them both write a `TargetVersion` — same path, different `source`.

**Renamed 20 Aug 2026** from `/api/onboarding/targets/` and `/api/targets/history/`; see the Decision Log.

* `onboarding` is a screen flow, not a resource, and the endpoint is not exclusive to it — settings recomputes proposals too. The thing being created is a *proposal*: a computed, unpersisted target set the user accepts or edits. Naming it after the caller would have meant renaming it the moment the second caller appeared
* `history/` and the bare collection are the same set. Targets are append-only (doc 02), so the collection *is* the history — two URLs for one list, where the extra one only exists because "history" is what the UI screen is called
* `current/` stays. A named singleton for the member the client can't address by id is legitimate REST, and "the version in effect now" is real state the server owns, unlike `today` in doc 07. It must be routed before `/api/targets/<int:pk>/` so the literal wins

## Adjusting targets later

* Editable at any time from settings
* Every change writes a new `TargetVersion`; nothing is updated in place
* Existing `DailyLog` rows keep pointing at their original version
* A history view showing targets over time makes the versioning tangible — and is genuinely interesting on a long cut

## UI notes

The AI call takes a few seconds. A frozen screen reads as a crash — the loading state matters.

The result screen shows three numbers plus the rationale, with **Accept** and **Adjust**. Never force acceptance of a generated number. Adjusting past the safe bounds is permitted, with the bounds shown.

## What you're learning

* Multi-step form state management in React Native
* Structured JSON output from an LLM, and validating rather than trusting it
* Defensive design around AI output where wrong answers matter
* The slowly-changing-dimension pattern in practice
* When *not* to use an LLM — the hybrid here is the concrete example
